text: Before you can write a meaningful C++ program, you need to understand what turns your source code into something the CPU can run. There's no interpreter reading your code line by line here — this lesson walks through the actual pipeline.

Three tools get lumped together, but they solve different problems. The compiler translates one source file into an object file, and only ever looks at that one file at a time. The linker combines object files and libraries into a final executable, resolving calls between them. And the build system decides which files to compile, in what order, with what flags, and recompiles only what changed. Past a handful of files, you need that last layer or you're typing the same command forever.

Every source file passes through four stages on the way to a running program. Preprocessing expands includes and macros. Compilation turns the preprocessed code into assembly for the target CPU. Assembly turns that into an object file — machine code, but not runnable yet. And linking stitches one or more object files together into the final executable.

You can actually run each of those stages yourself with separate compiler flags — stop after preprocessing, stop after compiling to assembly, stop after assembling, then link. In practice you'd never type all four; one command runs the whole pipeline. But knowing the stages exist matters the first time you hit a confusing linker error and need to know which stage actually failed.

Here's the command you'll actually type day to day. The standard flag picks which version of C++ you're targeting — this course uses seventeen and twenty throughout. The optimization flag matters once you start measuring performance. And the warning flags catch real bugs before they become mysterious crashes. Get comfortable with this command; you'll type some version of it constantly.

Compiler, linker, build system — three jobs, four stages, and for real projects, a tool like CMake running the whole thing instead of you typing commands by hand. Up next, lesson three: types, variables, and control flow, where you'll finally start writing the C++ that fills these files.
